item.title: How Trump Has Cracked Down on Dissent Since the Killing of Charlie Kirk
item.description:
The very public murder of Charlie Kirk on a Utah campus last September sent convulsions of grief through the political right. Within days, the Trump administration began transforming the slain prophet of young conservatives from a martyr to a cause.

“The last message that Charlie Kirk gave to me before he joined his creator in heaven was, he said, that we have to dismantle and take on the radical left organizations in this country that are fomenting violence,” Stephen Miller, a White House deputy chief of staff, said three days after the killing. “And we are going to do that.”

The message Mr. Miller described quickly turned into policy. Now, a year later, it is clear how bright a line of demarcation the period after Mr. Kirk’s death has become in the efforts by President Trump and his allies to target Americans they see as “the enemy within.”

The administration’s nearly exclusive crackdown on left-leaning organizations and activities has ushered in a pitched battle over political dissent and free speech.

Officials have taken a governmentwide approach to scrutinizing citizens and organizations opposed to Trump policies. Tax agents have examined nonprofit groups. Investigators have looked into the books of labor unions. Prosecutors have brought charges against anti-ICE protesters, asserting that a leftist conspiracy is provoking political violence on the streets.

These efforts came together this year in Minnesota, the scene of heated protests in response to the government’s aggressive immigration sweep. Federal investigators infiltrated neighborhood watch committees, church meetings and an environmental group in an operation that surveilled hundreds of ordinary people. Ultimately, 15 protesters were charged with conspiring to impede immigration enforcement as members of the far-left movement known as antifa, but prosecutors did not accuse them of any violent acts beyond kicking an ICE vehicle and sideswiping another.

When Paul Kirk-Davidoff, a meat cutter and union organizer in Minneapolis, saw in court files that undercover agents attended a meeting he had set up last February about resisting ICE, he said: “First I laughed, then I thought this is scary.”

From the start of his second term, Mr. Trump has wielded power to punish those he views as opponents, including law firms, universities, pro-Palestinian activists and news outlets, three of which he banned last week from the White House. But after the Kirk killing and assassination attempts on the president, Mr. Trump and his allies have recast the effort in existential terms.

“What we are finally coming to grips with on the right is that our opponents on the left, some of them, enough of them, want us dead,” Andrew Kolvet, a spokesman for Turning Point USA, Mr. Kirk’s conservative organization, said in an interview. “You have to deal with this or you are a sitting duck.”

Mr. Trump issued two directives soon after Mr. Kirk’s death that have guided the administration. On Sept. 22 last year, he signed an executive order designating antifa a domestic terrorist organization. Days later, he signed a national security document ordering an attack on what he said were networks that fomented political violence.

The motivating ideologies of these networks, the memo said, included “anti-Americanism, anti-capitalism, and anti-Christianity; support for the overthrow of the United States Government; extremism on migration, race, and gender; and hostility towards those who hold traditional American views on family, religion, and morality.”

Even though there is no provision in American law defining domestic terrorism and the F.B.I. has previously said that antifa is more of an antifascist ideology than an organization, the administration has attached both labels to protesters and some left-leaning groups.

The White House has defended the moves. “There is no safe harbor for those who illegally attack and obstruct law enforcement or wage campaigns of political violence against the American people,” said Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman.

But the administration’s campaign against violence is filtered through a political lens — alarming myriad organizations whose causes, from the environment to civil liberties to voting rights, are at odds with the president’s agenda.

Vanita Gupta, a New York University law professor and a former Biden-era Justice Department official, has organized nonprofit groups to counter what she said was the White House’s effort “to quell dissent, rewrite the past and suppress organizations that are challenging its narrative and policies.”

It is not just Democrats. An amicus brief filed last month in the Minnesota case by legal groups that included the libertarian Cato Institute and the right-leaning Society for the Rule of Law said Mr. Trump’s political violence directive, known as National Security Presidential Memorandum 7, “effectively uses the domestic-terrorism label to justify criminal investigations into disfavored groups that would not otherwise be targeted.”

American politics has been reshaped by belligerent, sometimes threatening, language on all sides and by heightened security concerns, underscored by the murders of Mr. Kirk and a Democratic lawmaker and her husband in Minnesota. While Mr. Trump’s allies say the left’s accusatory language encourages violence, demonizing on the right filters down from the Oval Office. In July, Mr. Miller described participants in “antifa protests” as “deformed in some way — in their appearance, in their dress, in their mannerism.”

Within days of the Kirk murder, Vice President JD Vance called for the punishment of anyone “celebrating” the shooting. Hundreds of people who criticized Mr. Kirk’s politics online lost or were threatened with losing their jobs.

The First Amendment protects nonviolent protests, but Mr. Trump has excused violent actions carried out on his behalf. Before pardoning nearly 1,600 participants in the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol riot, he said, “All they were doing was protesting a rigged election.”

For some, protesting has entailed more risk. Laurie and Richard Eckman, both in their 80s, found that out when they joined a demonstration in Portland, Ore. after Mr. Trump declared the city “war-ravaged” by “domestic terrorists” and ordered a stepped-up response.

Ms. Eckman, who first protested during the Vietnam era, said that as the matriarch of a multicultural family she objected to Mr. Trump’s treatment of immigrants. One day last fall, Mr. Eckman, a Vietnam veteran, grabbed his walker and the couple joined a march to the local ICE building.

When officers confronted the protesters, “I heard a loud bang and felt an extremely hard and direct impact” on her head, Ms. Eckman recalled. Bloodied by a pepper ball, she was treated in an emergency room for a concussion and breathing problems, she said.

“Unlike our more generalized protests against the Vietnam War,” she wrote later in her diary, “the threats to our democracy by this administration seem immediate and real and very personal.”

Within weeks of Mr. Trump issuing his security directives, prosecutors relied on them in a case that emerged from a July 4 “noise protest” at the Prairieland immigration detention center outside Dallas.

A group of leftist activists set off fireworks and scrawled anti-ICE graffiti on the facility. But one protester, a former Marine, shot and injured a police officer who had pointed a pistol at them.

Prosecutors had charged the 11 activists with attempted murder, but after Mr. Kirk’s killing, they filed different charges. They identified the defendants as “operatives” with the “North Texas Antifa Cell” and charged most of them with offering material support to terrorists — the first time terrorism statutes had been used against purported members of antifa. Those charges carried more severe penalties.

“As @POTUS has made clear,” Pam Bondi, then the attorney general, wrote on X at the time, “Antifa is a left-wing terrorist organization. They will be prosecuted as such.”

Almost immediately, critics — including some former terrorism prosecutors — expressed concern that the administration was using a vague definition of antifa to target people who had no clear connection beyond a shared ideology. They also said that even though the Prairieland protest had ended in gunfire, most of those facing charges had not committed violence.

One defendant, Daniel Sanchez Estrada, an elementary school aide who is married to another defendant, had not even been at the detention center when the shooting took place. The sole allegation against him was that he had concealed a box of anarchist zines, which the government presented as evidence of the defendants’ political beliefs.

He was sentenced to 30 years in prison. His eight co-defendants who went to trial were handed penalties totaling more than 400 years.

By late last year, the F.B.I. was moving forward with nearly 30 other investigations linked to the president’s directives, according to an internal memo. Agents from the bureau, the Department of Homeland Security and the Internal Revenue Service were working them through a “joint mission center” in Washington.

“Political violence is a scourge on our democracy, and it is increasingly organized, radical and dangerous,” a Justice Department spokesman said.

The success of the Prairieland prosecution influenced the investigation in Minnesota.

Last winter, masked ICE agents roamed the streets, pursuing undocumented immigrants, sometimes smashing car windows. Demonstrators massed outside the Whipple Building, the agency’s hub in Minneapolis. Local residents signed up to monitor ICE agents.

After two people, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were killed by federal agents, Mr. Miller and other administration officials labeled them domestic terrorists. The Justice Department declined to investigate Ms. Good’s killing and announced an inquiry into Mr. Pretti’s death only after public outcry.

But the department began scrutinizing demonstrators, homing in on left-leaning political groups that officials believed were funding protests.

Homeland Security investigators ramped up a surveillance operation that used undercover agents to infiltrate meetings where people were often recorded doing little more than expressing opinions, court records show.

“A heavy-set female approximately twenty-five (25) spoke about operational security,” one agent wrote about a February meeting at a library, the papers show. “The female warned attendees not to say anything in the meeting that you would not say to an ICE agent. The same female stated she had recently started a ‘Coffee Club’ where people can get to know each other on a more personal level.”

The investigators monitored protester group chats on Signal and took down license plate numbers of people who had voiced disdain for ICE agents, court records say.

In the funding inquiry, investigators obtained three years of financial records from two large mainstream labor unions and a climate action group, according to court documents.

In June, prosecutors charged 15 people, some with ties to those organizations, with impeding immigration enforcement as members of antifa. No allegations of wrongdoing by the unions or the climate group were made.

In announcing the case, Daniel Rosen, the U.S. attorney in Minnesota, said it was based on Mr. Trump’s security directives. “These defendants have been charged not for what they said but what they did,” he added.

The indictment said that on Jan. 23, some defendants threw ice at law enforcement vehicles at the Whipple Building and also tried to block agents from the building. Prosecutors did not allege that any of those charged had injured agents, and some had only joined meetings or online discussions.

One defendant, Erik Davis, a Macalester College religion professor, said in an interview that Minneapolis residents reacted to an “extreme and deadly” immigration sweep, but that “organizing protests, including very large ones, is not a crime.”

He said that he and his co-defendants were targets because of their activism, rooted in anarchism and radical labor politics.

“The government wants to use us to send a message to Americans that they shouldn’t dare to protest or oppose the regime or else you’ll be put on trial,” he said.

When a leader of the Southern Poverty Law Center, known for investigating extremist groups beginning with the Ku Klux Klan, appeared at a congressional hearing last spring, Representative Bob Onder, a Missouri Republican, confronted him. “Are you willing to take any responsibility for the assassination of Charlie Kirk?” he asked.

It was a made-for-viral moment, but it also reflected how the murder endures for many of Mr. Kirk’s MAGA admirers — both as a painful touchstone and a blunt instrument for attacking the left.

The basis for Mr. Onder’s question was the law center’s monthly “Trends and incidents of the hard right” report, published the day before Mr. Kirk’s death. It highlighted Turning Point’s association with Vince Everett Ellison, a virulent critic of diversity, equity and inclusion.

The law center had grown into a fund-raising juggernaut as the nation’s politics had become more divisive, adding groups to its “Hate Map” that Republicans considered mainstream. Even some on the left criticized its now retired founder, Morris Dees, of fund-raising off fear. “They were fast and loose in who they called a hate group,” Stephen B. Bright, a Yale law professor, said of the previous leadership.

In a May 2025 report, the law center accused Turning Point of “sowing and exploiting fear that white Christian supremacy is under attack” by immigrants, the L.G.B.T. community and civil rights activists. The report quoted Mr. Kirk: “You cannot have liberty if you don’t have a Christian population.”

In early September of last year, Mr. Kirk and others wrote to Mr. Miller, calling for action. They said the law center had become “biased, politicized and unmoored from its original mission,” as evidenced by its placing “traditional value and faith-based organizations” on its Hate Map.

After Mr. Kirk’s death, Elon Musk wrote on X, using the group’s initials: “SPLC is guilty of incitement to murder Charlie Kirk.” The next day, the F.B.I. director, Kash Patel, cut ties between his agency and the nonprofit group, which had worked together for decades to combat extremists.

In April, the Justice Department indicted the law center, alleging that by paying informants inside white supremacist organizations, it had defrauded its donors by promoting hate groups it said it was fighting.

The S.P.L.C. has defended itself by pointing out that the government has for years used information from the informants in criminal prosecutions. It tried to have the case dismissed, arguing that the prosecution was vindictive, aimed at silencing the group. A judge denied the request.

Like Mr. Kirk, the president has declared himself a defender of free speech, signing an executive order on Inauguration Day 2025 reaffirming “the right of the American People to speak freely” after the Biden administration “trampled speech rights.”

Jenin Younes, a lawyer who represented clients — including current Trump administration officials — censored on social media for posting what the Biden administration considered misinformation on Covid, said those free-speech violations were consequential.

“But you can’t compare that to bringing criminal charges, expelling people from universities, putting them behind bars and trying to deport them, ” said Ms. Younes, who now heads the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee. “The chilling effect of what the current administration has done is so much more severe.”

item.title: Many Democrats Are Avoiding Kamala Harris. Abdul El-Sayed Is Welcoming Her.
item.description:
In July, aides to former Vice President Kamala Harris circulated a document that showed how she would try to maintain her influence atop the Democratic Party as she considered another run for president in 2028.

The donor prospectus, which was obtained by The New York Times, listed how she might be helpful for midterm candidates and sought funding for her campaign travel. It also argued that the Supreme Court’s decision in April further eroding the Voting Rights Act, which allowed Southern states to eliminate majority-Black districts, would be a turnout machine for Black voters.

The current moment, the document states, is “uniquely suited to Vice President Harris and a broad coalition already in motion.” It adds, “What is needed is the operational funding to move the principal at the cadence required to Turn Out the Vote and win in November 2026.”

Democratic candidates, wary of campaigning with someone tied to the unpopular Biden administration, have not rushed to take Ms. Harris up on the offer. In recent weeks, Senate candidates in Alaska, Iowa and Kansas — states without large Black populations — have pre-emptively and publicly uninvited her from campaigning with them.

Several Democrats mentioned in the Harris donor document as candidates who could use her help do not appear eager, either. Aides to James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic nominees for the Senate and governor in Texas, as well as to Gov. Katie Hobbs in Arizona, told The Times that they did not want Ms. Harris to come.

But on Tuesday, Ms. Harris is set to make her first major campaign stop of the midterms, appearing in Michigan alongside Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the state’s Democratic nominee for the Senate.

The visit has the potential to be mutually beneficial for both Ms. Harris and Dr. El-Sayed.

For Ms. Harris, the trip will be a high-profile appearance in a top Senate race. Dr. El-Sayed is also one of her party’s leading pro-Palestinian figures, which could help her move beyond the Biden administration’s support of Israel during the war in Gaza, an approach that became unpopular with many Democratic voters.

For Dr. El-Sayed, who needs to shore up support from Black voters and moderates skeptical of his fiery progressive politics, the appearance with Ms. Harris will give him a seal of approval from a prominent Black Democrat and an establishment leader in the party.

After her Michigan stop, she is scheduled to appear in Nevada with Aaron Ford, the state’s Democratic attorney general, who is running for governor, and in California with two Democratic House candidates vying to flip seats. Later this fall, on the Friday before the midterms, she is set to appear in Georgia with Senator Jon Ossoff, another top Democratic candidate for the Senate.

“Right now, midterms, midterms, midterms, full time, occupying my thoughts, my mind and my work,” Ms. Harris said recently on a podcast hosted by the former soccer star Megan Rapinoe. “We have to win these midterms.”

Michigan has presented both Ms. Harris and Dr. El-Sayed with thorny political challenges.

Dr. El-Sayed narrowly won an ugly primary against Representative Haley Stevens, who had far more financial support and drew much stronger backing from the state’s Black voters. Ever since, he has been trying to unite Democrats against his Republican opponent, former Representative Mike Rogers.

Ms. Harris and the Biden administration, for their part, faced the fiercest pushback over the war in Gaza in Michigan, which has large populations of Arab and Muslim voters. Ms. Harris narrowly lost the state in 2024.

Dr. El-Sayed, who endorsed the “Uncommitted” movement of primary protest votes against President Joseph R. Biden Jr. in 2024, acknowledged on MS Now last week that some Black Michiganders had “hurt feelings” about that effort. Ms. Harris, he said, would be the ideal person to vouch for his campaign.

“She understood just how frustrating that moment was and the challenges with, with the Biden-era policy toward Gaza going into 2024,” Dr. El-Sayed said. “This is an opportunity for us to come together.”

Ms. Harris is scheduled to make two public stops on Tuesday in Detroit. She will participate in a discussion on Black maternal health with Dr. El-Sayed and appear at a forum on voting rights with the local N.A.A.C.P. chapter.

Hasan Piker, the provocative left-wing streamer who has sharply criticized Ms. Harris’s foreign policy positions and caused political headaches for Dr. El-Sayed, commended her for going to Michigan.

“Older Black voters, they love Kamala Harris,” Mr. Piker said on his stream last weekend. “This is not about agreeing with Kamala Harris, this is not about her positions. The question always is: Do you want to win? And if you want to win, you have to do this.”

Ms. Harris may also face pressure from pro-Israel Democrats in Michigan, which has many Jewish voters as well. A group of local rabbis who two weeks ago pressed Dr. El-Sayed to change his stance and tone on Israel sent a letter to Ms. Harris on Tuesday urging her to reiterate her support for the country. “You have never let us wonder whether our safety mattered to you,” the rabbis wrote.

An aide to Ms. Harris said she did not plan to address the approach to Israel she backed as vice president but did not discount the possibility that the issue could come up.

Several high-profile Democratic midterm candidates have made the calculation that they would rather do without Ms. Harris’s help.

Her attempt to raise money online for former Representative Mary Peltola in Alaska fell flat when Ms. Peltola denounced the assistance. In Iowa, the party’s candidates for the Senate and governor said they did not want her to campaign with them. And in Kansas, Adam Hamilton, the Democratic candidate for the Senate, told Politico that he needed to appeal to Republicans, whose “worldview may be a bit different than Kamala Harris.”

All of those states, notably, have small Black populations.

The Harris document for donors suggests that she could be helpful to several Democrats in more racially diverse states: former Gov. Roy Cooper of North Carolina, who is running for the Senate; Ms. Hobbs in Arizona; and Mr. Talarico and Ms. Hinojosa in Texas.

None have any plans to campaign with Ms. Harris.

In North Carolina, Kate Smart, a spokeswoman for Mr. Cooper, said there had been no talks with Ms. Harris’s team about her campaigning with him there.

In Texas, Mr. Talarico will not campaign with Ms. Harris or any other potential 2028 White House aspirant, an aide said. Ms. Hinojosa’s spokesman, Tommy Kubitschek, said that aides for “several other” potential presidential candidates, but not Ms. Harris’s, had reached out. “Gina is focused on Texas and Texans,” he said.

And in Arizona, Ms. Hobbs has not been in touch with Ms. Harris and is not asking her to come campaign with her, said Michael Beyer, the governor’s communications director.

During a phone interview on MS Now this month, Ms. Harris was asked about red-state Democrats who had publicly rejected her. “I support them in doing whatever they need to do to win,” she said.

“Vice President Harris will travel to multiple states over the coming weeks,” said her spokesman, Eduardo Negrón. “In some, she will campaign directly alongside candidates, as she will this week in Michigan. In others, she has been asked by state parties and voter protection groups to help register and mobilize voters.”

Ms. Harris also spoke last month at a state party fund-raising dinner in Louisiana. And she has been in talks with Wisconsin Democrats about holding get-out-the-vote events during the final stretch before Election Day. Devin Remiker, the chairman of the state Democratic Party, said she is welcome.

“We’d be thrilled to have her and anybody else ready to help us energize and mobilize voters to win a Democratic trifecta this November,” he said.

Ms. Harris has said little about her 2028 plans since she revealed in April that she was “thinking about” running for president again. Early polls show her as a Democratic front-runner, though that status is largely based on name recognition.

Last week, another potential candidate, Gov. Gavin Newsom of California, said that he would not run for president if Ms. Harris did.

In the meantime, she will face heightened interest in her midterm movements.

In addition to campaigning in Nevada with Mr. Ford, the Democratic candidate for governor, she will appear with two Democrats trying to flip Republican-held congressional seats in California — Marni von Wilpert in the San Diego area and Dr. Richard Pan in Northern California.

But none of those candidates or their aides agreed to interview requests about Ms. Harris’s upcoming visits.

Ms. Harris has also announced that just before the midterms, she will appear in Georgia with Mr. Ossoff and speak at a fund-raising dinner for the Democratic Party of Fulton County.

Kayla Garthus, the county’s Democratic chairwoman, said it was a “no-brainer” to invite Ms. Harris to help with voter turnout efforts in the campaign’s final days.

Georgia has battleground contests for the Senate, where Mr. Ossoff is seeking re-election, and governor, in which former Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms of Atlanta faces Rick Jackson, a wealthy Republican businessman.

“We see it as an opportunity for Fulton County Democrats running,” Ms. Garthus said. “We do feel strongly that her presence should help bolster turnout for sure and hopefully get some of our local candidates the highlights they deserve.”

item.title: San Francisco Sues to Stop Early Access to Trump’s Truth Social Posts
item.description:
San Francisco has filed a lawsuit to try to stop the social media platform Truth Social from giving users early access to President Trump’s posts if they pay up to $100,000 each month.

David Chiu, the San Francisco city attorney, filed the lawsuit on Monday against Trump Media & Technology Group, which owns Truth Social, arguing that the program violated California’s Unfair Competition Law because it gave wealthy traders an early look at government information, leaving out everyday investors.

“They have knowingly created a marketplace for insider trading,” Mr. Chiu told The New York Times in an interview. “This scheme has turned the public trust into private profit, and it is corruption at the highest level of government.”

On July 17, Trump Media announced its new paid service on Truth Social called Truth API. As of early August, users could pay up to $100,000 a month for a new data feed offering an early view of posts from Mr. Trump and other prominent users, including Vice President JD Vance and Donald Trump Jr., the president’s oldest son. Participants get only a head start of a fraction of a second, but that is enough time for firms that use algorithmic programs to make instant stock trades.

Mr. Trump is the largest shareholder in Trump Media. He co-founded Truth Social after he was blocked from other social media sites for his role in the Jan. 6, 2021 attack at the U.S. Capitol.

Mr. Trump has posted thousands of times on the platform since then, sometimes racking up dozens of posts per day. He often makes announcements in all capital letters and signs off with, “Thank you for your attention to this matter,” followed by his initials.

In a statement on Monday, a spokesman for Trump Media said: “The people of California should outsource their future lawsuits to AI chatbots who, unlike the left-wing activists masquerading as attorneys who filed this lawsuit, will grasp the basic distinction between public and nonpublic information.”

Mr. Chiu said that while hedge funds and cryptocurrency firms could benefit from paying the Truth Social fee, Californians with investments in 401(k) retirement accounts, 529 education accounts, public pension plans and other stock holdings would suffer.

Mr. Chiu’s lawsuit in San Francisco Superior Court argues that many of the president’s past Truth Social posts have moved the stock market.

The suit singles out one from April 9, 2025, in which Mr. Trump posted, “THIS IS A GREAT TIME TO BUY!!! DJT.” Hours later, Mr. Trump announced that he was pausing tariffs on most countries for 90 days, after which the stock market increased in value.

On June 11, Mr. Trump posted that he would hit Iran “VERY HARD, TONIGHT,” and crude-oil futures surged.

Despite the president’s regular pronouncements, interest in Truth Social has fallen off. The number of monthly visitors in July was down 36 percent from the previous year. Trump Media has also struggled, posting a net loss of $238.1 million in the second quarter of this year.

Numerous Democrats and some Republicans in Congress have criticized the Truth API program. At least two lawmakers, Senator Mark Warner, Democrat of Virginia, and Senator Alex Padilla, Democrat of California, have proposed legislation to ban it.

Trump Media representatives have disputed that the program amounts to insider trading. Kevin McGurn, the company’s interim chief executive, said in a conference call with investors last month that “customers will get published and publicly available posts fractionally faster” than others and called it a “well-established business practice.”

Another lawsuit against the service was filed last month in federal court, arguing that the First Amendment guaranteed equal access to public information unless there was a “legitimate government purpose” for restricting it. That suit, filed by the Freedom of the Press Foundation and The Intercept, named Mr. Trump and other White House officials as defendants; the San Francisco suit targets Trump Media.

Mr. Chiu, a former Democratic state lawmaker, argued that Truth Social was selling early access at the same time that Mr. Trump was making it more difficult for the public to obtain information. He pointed to the president’s recent banning of CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House.

“The fact that this has been allowed to happen is astonishing,” Mr. Chiu said.

San Francisco’s mayor, Daniel Lurie, has avoided confrontation with Mr. Trump, often refusing to say the president’s name. But Mr. Chiu has consistently been waging legal battles against the president, filing 19 previous lawsuits against the administration since January 2025 challenging policies on matters ranging from birthright citizenship to sanctuary cities.

item.title: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez on 2028: ‘Life Doesn’t Wait for You to Be Ready’
item.description:
Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has said she will weigh the decision of whether to run for president after the midterm elections. The decision is clearly already weighing on her.

In an interview with The New York Times, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez revealed the electoral equations she is crunching and the mental “math” she is calculating as she approaches the biggest crossroads of her political career.

Her gender. Her ethnicity. Her electability. Her eggs. Her movement. Her moment.

“There’s an argument that some make that this is a very unique political window and, oftentimes in politics, you do only get one shot,” she said. “And you don’t — and just in life in general — life doesn’t wait for you to be ready for things. Sometimes life just makes things ready for you.”

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez, 36, the youngest woman ever elected to Congress, is now in her eighth year representing parts of the Bronx and Queens. She could simply keep winning re-election. But in 2028, she has two other choices: run for the White House, or seek the seat now held by Senator Chuck Schumer of New York.

“Every element of this is something that’s within consideration,” she said.

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez weighed aloud the pros and cons of running for president with unusual candor, sounding less strategic than searching, as if the right answer were somewhere nearby.

At times, she played the part of political pundit handicapping her own potential presidential candidacy from afar. At others, she voiced the unvarnished concerns of a woman who just opened up on Instagram (“Bloat check!”) about fertility treatments preparing for a possible future pregnancy.

“I think about it personally,” she said of a White House run. “I am 36, I’m about to turn 37 years old — and what that means for my life.”

“Pretty candidly, I think about my identity,” Ms. Ocasio-Cortez went on. “I’m not naïve to the fact that we are living under a very regressive administration, and I happen to be a woman, and I, you know, happen to be Latina. And I think that there’s a lot of conversation about electability, and I don’t kind of shy away from those realities.”

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez arrived in Congress as a left-wing outsider and remains one of the party’s most progressive voices. Some party strategists are urging Democrats to move to the middle. But Ms. Ocasio-Cortez was heartened by “the ascendance for the first time” of progressives like Dr. Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan who toppled big-money candidates in this year’s Senate primaries.

“I have a tremendous amount of fear over the corruption of our political system,” she said.

She spoke by phone last week as she recovered in her Washington apartment from Covid. She had called to discuss an upcoming swing through upstate New York and a cash transfer to help Democrats in her home state.

She wound up describing much more.

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez knows that broaching the roles of race and gender in politics can be unpopular, even unappealing. “I often hesitate to even talk about it,” she said, “because people then just register it as an excuse or a complaint.”

She is talking about it anyway.

“If you’re asking me about the things that I weigh, of course, that’s part of what I weigh,” she said of running for president as a woman. “It’s funny because it’s kind of like, everyone else is allowed to talk about it, but I’m not?”

She described the gender gap as a fact of American electoral politics: Roughly 27 percent of Congress is female, she said, and 0 percent of past presidents.

It’s not just that a five-second video of her adjusting her hair in the Bronx this year drew more than 25 million views on X and a tsunami of sexualized replies (“that’s the most kind of, like, brazen and obvious forms of it,” she said). It’s how “female politicians are discussed, approached, covered” overall.

“What is very odd about our political culture is that for some reason when you raise it, people just freak out,” she said. “They get so defensive at the mere suggestion that gender could play a role.”

She made plain that this was a problem “independent of ideology.”

“I experience it tremendously — from the right and from the left,” she said.

The losses of the only two women ever to secure the Democratic presidential nomination, Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris, loom large. “It may or may not be related, but I absolutely empathize with the heartbreak that people feel around that and, frankly, how those women were treated,” Ms. Ocasio-Cortez said.

She said she had discussed the issue with Ms. Harris, who is also considering a 2028 run, but she declined to describe their private conversations.

“This country has never elected a female president. Why are we pretending that this is not a factor?” Ms. Ocasio-Cortez said with a laugh. “That doesn’t make it impossible, but to act as though it’s not a factor in anything ever is really a form of, like, denialism.”

Few politicians can command public attention like Ms. Ocasio-Cortez. Her egg-freezing set off a national conversation about fertility. Her offhand remark on ABC News that “Woke one was crazy” spawned a thousand takes on her thinking and her party’s evolution.

No matter the size of her megaphone, it is also true that no House member has ascended directly to the presidency in modern history. (Few see any applicable lessons in the election of James A. Garfield in 1880.) Even if she is one of the House’s most prolific fund-raisers, a potential attempted leap to the White House would be essentially unprecedented.

The Senate seat in New York could be an alluring alternative.

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez, who won her seat by toppling a powerful Democratic House leader in a 2018 primary, did not rule out the possibility of challenging Mr. Schumer — even if he helps Democrats win a Senate majority in the midterms.

“That would honestly be the best possible problem we could have as a country,” she said of the idea that a Democratic Senate majority could further complicate her 2028 choices. She added, “We’re working hard to have that problem, and I’ll cross that bridge when I get to it.”

Mr. Schumer, 75, has not announced his own 2028 plans.

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez made this much clear: She is not waiting on anyone other than herself, whether that pits her as a primary challenger to a potential Senate majority leader or to a former vice president.

“I don’t think that my decisions would come down to deference,” she said.

Back in May, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez went viral for an answer she gave at a forum with David Axelrod, the onetime adviser to former President Barack Obama, in which she said her ambitions were not a “title or a seat.”

“My ambition is way bigger than that,” she said. “My ambition is to change this country. Presidents come and go, Senate, House seats, elected officials come and go, but single-payer health care is forever, a living wage is forever, workers’ rights are forever, women’s rights, all of that.”

Mr. Axelrod said in an interview that he believed Ms. Ocasio-Cortez when she spoke about her motivations.

“She is very honest in her communications. It’s what makes her disarming,” he said. “Her bottom line is producing something for the people she’s fighting for, so I think this decision is partly seen through that prism.”

In her interview with The Times, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez repeated variations of that line about her lack of interest in “my title.” But she also expressed a keen awareness of the realities that House members must seek re-election every two years and that losing would mean being out of office entirely.

“It’s very all or nothing,” she said. “If I were to run in this cycle, and not win, I would be done.”

“And I am not opposed to that,” she added. But it was also a consideration. “That, in and of itself, does not exclude the decision,” she finally said. “But it has to make it worth it.”

Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, her mentor and ally, is 85. Many on the left see Ms. Ocasio-Cortez as his natural successor. The two politicians’ “Fighting Oligarchy” tour in 2025 drew huge crowds.

“These rallies were bigger than the sum of their parts,” Ms. Ocasio-Cortez said. “When Bernie was on his own, or when I’m on my own, it’s different because we have overlapping but also complementary coalitions.”

In other words, she is thinking about the political coalition of Mr. Sanders, the runner-up in the last two open Democratic presidential primaries — and how it might intersect with her own.

Mr. Sanders had advantages that Ms. Ocasio-Cortez does not. His 2016 run made him a national figure on the left before the right took to attacking him. Ms. Ocasio-Cortez has been a boogeywoman for Republicans almost since her arrival on the scene in 2018, and she would be the Democratic Party’s most progressive standard-bearer in decades, if not ever.

In a recent New York Times/Siena University poll, her favorable rating among Republicans was less than 1 percent — with 75 percent rating her unfavorably.

Overall, just 30 percent of likely voters nationally viewed her favorably, with 41 percent holding an unfavorable opinion.

Her democratic socialist ally, Zohran Mamdani, the mayor of New York City, had a higher favorable rating, 38 percent, and a lower unfavorable rating, 33 percent. (Born in Uganda, Mr. Mamdani is not eligible to serve as president.)

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez hailed Mr. Mamdani, 34, as “an incredible political talent.”

“There are also major differences between an executive position for a municipal seat and a legislative position,” she said, which regularly sets up “conflict with your peers.”

“Of course, obviously, there are…” she paused. “I don’t know why it’s controversial to say that there are headwinds in identity and gender.”

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez is not just a good fund-raiser. She has raised $32 million from January 2025 to July 2026 — more than double the sum that any other House incumbent raised in their re-election account other than Speaker Mike Johnson or Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the Democratic leader.

She is prideful of her almost exclusive dependence on small donors.

“I have a tremendous amount of fear over the corruption of our political system,” she said. “There’s very few people who are financially independent from special interests that are able to advocate directly for the needs of working people.”

In the end, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez landed on the most familiar of lines to described the driving force behind her 2028 decision.

“Where can I do the most good?”

item.title: Videos Reveal New Details About ICE Shooting in Austin
item.description:
Shortly before 1 p.m. on Sunday, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer opened fire on a blue Toyota Corolla after an apparent car chase and collision in northwestern Austin, Texas. The driver suffered a gunshot wound, according to Robert Luckritz, the chief of Austin-Travis County Emergency Medical Services.

While it remains unclear exactly what happened in the moments leading up to the shooting of Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, visual and audio evidence synchronized and analyzed by The New York Times shows that an ICE officer was standing to the side of the car, which was rolling forward, when the officer apparently fired through the rear passenger window. Footage shows Mr. Garces Perez with a wound on his back.

No other officers were visible near the car at the time of the shooting. Mr. Garces Perez was taken to a nearby hospital and is being held at an ICE detention facility.

Mr. Garces Perez, who is a Venezuelan immigrant, was not the target of an immigration operation, according to two people familiar with the shooting, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak about the investigation. ICE officers in the area were checking license plates when they discovered that he had a deportation order on file, the people said.

The officers pulled Mr. Garces Perez’s car over at about 12:45 p.m. on Sunday while he was making DoorDash deliveries. They told him that they were ICE officers and that he was going to be arrested. Mr. Garces Perez fled in his car after that, the two people familiar with the shooting said.

A short chase ensued before ICE officers encountered Mr. Garces Perez again, the two people said. The shooting occurred after that.

The Department of Homeland Security said in a post on social media that Homeland Security Investigations, with the assistance of the F.B.I., was investigating the shooting. The department did not respond to questions about the shooting.

A video livestreamed on Facebook with a cellphone’s front-facing camera at approximately 12:48 p.m. briefly catches Mr. Garces Perez’s blue Toyota Corolla on a busy boulevard. An S.U.V. appears to be driving toward the Toyota’s passenger side. The audio from the livestream, which was out of sync in the original post, was synchronized by The Times.

Sirens blare and tires screech as the person filming switches to the cellphone’s main camera, causing the image to freeze briefly. It is unclear if the two vehicles made contact at this moment. When the video resumes, Mr. Garces Perez’s Toyota has not moved far, but it is now facing an entirely different direction. Pulled alongside it is an unmarked Ford S.U.V. driven by a federal immigration officer.

Photographs and videos recorded moments later show serious damage to the passenger side of the Toyota. Mr. Garces Perez said over the phone at a news conference that a federal vehicle hit his car twice before an ICE officer fired at him.

The livestreamed video shows an officer exiting the driver’s side of the unmarked S.U.V. and circling around to the rear passenger side of the Toyota with his arms raised and pointed toward the vehicle. The immigration officer remains to the side of the car as it rolls forward slowly. No other officers are seen standing at or near the front of the Toyota.

According to an audio analysis by Robert C. Maher, a gunfire acoustics expert at Montana State University in Bozeman, Mont., four gunshots are audible. The Toyota continues rolling forward slowly before coming to a stop. The video then shows the officer running to the driver’s side of the car.

The officer’s weapon is not clearly visible in the footage when the shots are heard. Photographs taken later of the Toyota show two holes in the rear passenger window. The location of the holes appears to align with where the officer was standing when shots were fired.

Footage recorded moments after the shots shows Mr. Garces Perez remaining seated in the driver’s seat, where he applies pressure to his left shoulder with his hand.

An officer wearing a vest marked “ERO” — denoting the Enforcement and Removal Operations branch of ICE — then walks from the unmarked S.U.V. back to the driver’s side of the Toyota, holding a phone to his ear.

Another video filmed more than six minutes after the gunshots rang out shows Mr. Garces Perez still in the Toyota, holding his shoulder without any signs of medical assistance.

Around 12:55 p.m., Austin police officers arrive on the scene. Much of the conversation is hard to make out, but one Austin officer can be heard asking an ICE officer, “He hit you?”

"Yeah,” the ICE officer replies. The rest of his response is unclear.

A few seconds later the Austin officer asks, “You shot him?”

“Yeah,” the ICE officer replied. The rest of the response is not clear. A few seconds later, he tells the local officer that E.M.S. in on the way.

Shortly after approaching Mr. Garces Perez, one of the police officers runs back to his vehicle and rummages around in its trunk. He returns with what appears to be a first-aid kit tucked under his arm, while pulling on rubber gloves. His partner and a Texas Department of Public Safety trooper remove Mr. Garces Perez from the car while an ICE officer handcuffs him. They seat him on the curb. A wound is visible in Mr. Garces Perez’s upper back.

It is approximately eight minutes after the shooting.

It’s unclear from the available footage what happens in the next few minutes.

According to Mr. Luckritz, the Austin-Travis County E.M.S. chief, an ambulance arrived around 1 p.m. Images taken shortly after it arrived show emergency workers unloading a stretcher from the back of the vehicle.

Mr. Garces Perez was taken to a hospital, and according to his attorney, was discharged and is being held at the South Texas ICE Processing Center in Pearsall, Texas.

The episode is the latest in a string of shootings by federal immigration agents during the Trump administration’s crackdown: At least 24 people have been shot at, some of them fatally. This year, federal agents shot and killed Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis; Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston; and Johan Sebastian Durán Guerrero in Biddeford, Maine.

Hamed Aleaziz and Sam Lerma contributed reporting.
